fixes.explanation: I get why you'd pick it, since lions and roaring go together like dough and a hot oven. But the LORD never mentions roaring here. He asks about hunting the prey for a lioness and satisfying the hunger of young lions (Job 38:39).
Yes, friend. The text says the raven's young "…cry out to God as they wander about for lack of food?" (Job 38:41). The LORD asks who provides food for the raven. God is the One they cry out to.

Crying out to the wind sounds poetic, but that's not what the text says. The young ravens cry out to God as they wander about for lack of food (Job 38:41). Crying out to the wind would be like leaving a message for a stranger on the wrong phone number. These little ones cry out to the right One.
That's what He says. The LORD tells Job, "I made the wilderness his home and the salt flats his dwelling." (Job 39:6). That's a pretty big backyard for one donkey.

That sounds sensible, but training never comes up in the LORD's questions. He asks if the wild ox will consent to serve Job and if Job can hold him to the furrow with a harness (Job 39:9-10). The answer these questions point to is that Job can't make him serve.

Wisdom is a fine word, but this verse says strength. The LORD asks if Job can rely on the wild ox's great strength, then if he will leave his hard work to him (Job 39:11). I'd think twice before handing my stamping job to something that big.
The text never says a word about beauty in this part. It says "…God has deprived her of wisdom; He has not endowed her with understanding." (Job 39:17). Wisdom is what the verse names as missing.

Camels are tough, but they're not in this verse. The text says that when the ostrich proudly spreads her wings, she laughs at the horse and its rider (Job 39:18). I bet that's one confident bird, laughing at a whole horse.

You've got it. The text says, "He catches the scent of battle from afar, the shouts of captains and the cry of war." (Job 39:25). That's a horse with a pretty sharp nose, I think. Afar is a long way off.
The text says the opposite, friend. The war horse "…catches the scent of battle from afar, the shouts of captains and the cry of war." (Job 39:25). Afar is exactly where the text says he catches it.

Right on the money. The LORD asks, "Does the hawk take flight by your understanding…" and "Does the eagle soar at your command…" (Job 39:26-27). Each question points to the same answer: Job isn't the one behind it. The hawk's flight and the eagle's soaring don't come from his understanding or his command.

That's a big claim, friend. The LORD asks if the hawk takes flight by Job's understanding (Job 39:26). He asks if the eagle soars at Job's command (Job 39:27). Those questions point to a no, so Job isn't the one directing their flight.
An offering is a fair guess, but it isn't in this verse. The LORD says, "Let him who argues with God give an answer." (Job 40:2). The one who argues with God is the one being asked for the answer.

That's the word, friend. Job says, "Behold, I am insignificant. How can I reply to You?" (Job 40:4). It comes after all those questions about lions, ravens and horses. Then he says he places his hand over his mouth.
Weary is an understandable guess, but it's not the word Job uses. He says, "Behold, I am insignificant. How can I reply to You?" (Job 40:4). The word is insignificant.
A robe is a good guess, but it's not in the verse. Job says, "I place my hand over my mouth." (Job 40:4). I think a hand over the mouth says a lot with no words.
A sleeve would be a clever move, but the text says something simpler. Job says, "I place my hand over my mouth." (Job 40:4). It's his hand that goes over his mouth.
I can see why you'd think so, friend. But here Job says he has "…nothing to add." (Job 40:5). He has spoken once but has no answer, and twice but has nothing to add. So he's not adding anything.

That's right, friend. Job tells the LORD he has spoken once but has no answer, and twice but has "…nothing to add." (Job 40:5). After the LORD's questions about the animals, Job has no answer and nothing to add.
